content.title: About
content.content: Chamomile tea is an infusion of dried chamomile flowers (Matricaria chamomilla), usually served hot. It has a mild, slightly sweet flavor and an apple‑like aroma. The drink is popular as a calming beverage, especially in the evening.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chamomile has been used in traditional medicine for over 4,000 years.
Several species exist; the most common is German chamomile (Matricaria recutita).
Ancient Egyptians used chamomile to dye fabrics.
Chamomile tea is often offered in hotels and restaurants as a non‑alcoholic alternative.
Its scent is believed to help improve sleep quality.

items.title: Calms the nervous system
items.content: Flavonoids such as apigenin in chamomile promote relaxation and may reduce anxiety.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: A warm infusion stimulates bile production and can ease stomach cramps.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory effect
items.content: Antioxidants in chamomile help lower inflammation throughout the body.

items.title: Soothes cold symptoms
items.content: Heat and aroma can relieve nasal congestion and cough.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Flavonoids protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Asteraceae allergy
items.content: People allergic to plants of the Asteraceae family (e.g., daisies) may react to chamomile.

items.title: Drug interactions
items.content: Chamomile can enhance the effects of sedatives and anticoagulants.

items.title: Pregnancy
items.content: Large amounts of chamomile tea are not recommended for pregnant women without medical advice.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Place 1‑2 teaspoons of dried flowers into 200 ml of boiling water, steep for 5‑10 minutes, then strain. Drink hot, optionally sweetened with honey or a slice of lemon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dried flowers in an airtight container in a cool, dry, dark place. Shelf life is typically 1‑2 years. Discard if you notice mold odor or loss of aroma.
